new_statements.quote: 5.3.1 Stress: there is one degree of phonemic stress, /'/, which occurs on the first or second syllable of 2 or 3 syllable words; and on the first, second, or third of 4 syllable words. 5.3.2 The following contrasts have been found:- /'faga/ 'pretence' /fa'ga/ 'root vegetable' ... /'kafe/ 'door' /ka'fa/ 'rat' [Note: This analysis was based on nouns of up to 4 syllables.] ... 5.3.3 A non-phonemic, secondary stress occurs in words of more than 3 syllables and is always two syllables removed from the primary stress placement. ... 5.3.4 A shift of stress: a change of stress placement has been observed in some instances. However, since this always occurs in conjunction with morphological or intonational changes, it has not been included in this statement.
new_statements.citation: Young, Robert & Rosemary Young. 1961. The phonemes of Bena-Bena (a routine statement). SIL manuscript, Ukarumpa (SIL PNG Language Resources archive 51603).
new_statements.check: confirmed by a second reader, with minor differences
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: File check: (34-page image-only scan, Adobe 2009, no text layer) plus the held tesseract text. I rendered PDF pp. 18-19 (ms pp. 17-18) to PNG and read them directly. Sec. 5.3 'Supra-segmental Items' is exactly where stated. 5.3.1 reads verbatim: 'Stress: there is one degree of phonemic stress, /'/, which occurs on the first or second syllable of 2 or 3 syllable * words; and on the first, second, or third of 4 syllable words.' with footnote '* Note: This analysis was based on nouns of up to 4 syllables.' 5.3.2 lists the stress-only pairs /'faga/ ('faga) 'pretence' vs /fa'ga/ (fa'ga) 'root vegetable', /'abi/ 'yam' vs /a'bi/ 'a white sweet-potato', /se'gitabe/ 'a flower' vs /segi'tabe/ 'centip…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is phonemic (lexically contrastive): a single primary stress may fall on the 1st or 2nd syllable of di- and trisyllabic nouns and on the 1st, 2nd or 3rd syllable of quadrisyllabic nouns, with minimal pairs distinguished by stress alone; it is never reported on the final syllable of 3-4-syllable words. Confirmed by the 1992/2004 SIL OPD ('Stress is phonemic, but is not written') and Young 1975 ('Stress, phonemically distinguishable, is not marked').
new_statements.secondary_stress: Non-phonemic secondary stress in words of more than three syllables, always two syllables away from the primary (e.g. 'heto"fana 'good', "segi'tabe 'centipede', 'imi"ma?i 'earthquake'), i.e. an alternating rhythm anchored on the lexical primary.
new_statements.exceptions: Stress shifts under inflection and intonation were observed but excluded; the analysis covers only simple uninflected nouns of up to 4 syllables (words run to 8 syllables). Sec. 8.1: when adjacent syllables have identical vowels and stress is on the second, the first (unstressed) vowel is extremely short.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level, citation forms of uninflected nouns; the word is defined (6.1.2) as the unit bearing exactly one primary stress; the syllable (6.1.1) is 'a unit of actual or potential stress placement'.
new_statements.identity_note: Young & Young 1961 describe Bena-bena as spoken just east of Goroka (SIL work based at Segeya per the 1992 OPD); language-level bena1264, no sub-dialect singled out. The 1961 stress analysis is explicitly restricted to simple uninflected nouns of up to 4 syllables.
